ABSTRACT The growing availability of digital legal documents has made it increasingly difficult to locate relevant legal provisions and court judgments. Traditional keyword-based search methods often fail to identify information that is similar in meaning but expressed differently. In addition, standalone Large Language Models (LLMs) may generate answers that contain unsupported information or hallucinated details. To address these issues, this project introduces Legal RAG, a context-aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation system developed to answer questions using information retrieved from legal documents. The system begins by extracting text from uploaded PDF files, using OCR when documents contain scanned pages.

The system begins by extracting text from uploaded PDF files, using OCR when documents contain scanned pages. The extracted content is then divided into hierarchy-aware chunks that retain section headings and relevant legal metadata. These chunks are converted into embeddings using nomic-embed-text and stored in a persistent ChromaDB collection. When a user submits a question, the system performs hybrid retrieval by combining dense semantic search with BM25-based keyword search. The resulting rankings are combined through Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) and further refined using the ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 Cross-Encoder reranker. A two-layer query classifier determines the intent and complexity of each question and adjusts the retrieval process accordingly. For more complex queries, the system can perform up to three retrieval rounds to gather additional context.

For more complex queries, the system can perform up to three retrieval rounds to gather additional context. The final response is generated using the openai/gpt-oss-20b model through Groq, with retrieved document content serving as the basis for the answer. A citation-verification module checks whether individual claims are supported by valid references to retrieved chunks. Through the Streamlit interface, users can view generated answers along with their supporting passages, retrieval scores, and claim-level verification results. The system was evaluated using 25 automated tests covering query classification, retrieval control, document indexing, embedding validation, citation verification, and explainability. The evaluation indicates that combining semantic and keyword-based retrieval helps the system handle both concept based questions and queries involving specific legal terms.

The evaluation indicates that combining semantic and keyword-based retrieval helps the system handle both concept based questions and queries involving specific legal terms. Citation verification also improves the traceability of generated responses by linking claims to their supporting sources. Overall, Legal RAG is designed to make searching and understanding legal documents more accessible while serving as an assistive tool rather than a replacement for professional legal advice. CHAPTER 1 INTRODUCTION

1.1 Background of Study The rapid advancement of information technology has significantly transformed the way information is created, stored, and accessed. A considerable amount of information is now available in digital form, including legal documents such as court judgments, statutes, acts, regulations, contracts, legal notices, and case reports. These documents contain essential information concerning legal rights, obligations, judicial decisions, and established procedures. However, the increasing volume and complexity of digital legal information have made the process of locating relevant content more challenging. Legal documents are generally extensive in length and often contain specialized terminology, complex sentence structures, and detailed references to different provisions. Identifying a particular legal principle or provision may require users to examine several documents and interpret information distributed across multiple sections.

Identifying a particular legal principle or provision may require users to examine several documents and interpret information distributed across multiple sections. This process can be time-consuming, particularly for individuals who do not have extensive knowledge of legal terminology or document structures. In a country such as India, where the legal framework includes numerous central and state laws along with judicial precedents, efficient access to relevant legal information is especially important. Conventional information retrieval systems primarily depend on keyword matching to identify relevant documents. Although these systems are effective when users know the exact terms or phrases they are searching for, they often have difficulty understanding the underlying meaning of a query. Consequently, documents that are contextually relevant may remain undiscovered when they use terminology different from that of the user's question.

Consequently, documents that are contextually relevant may remain undiscovered when they use terminology different from that of the user's question. This limitation creates a need for retrieval systems capable of understanding both the language and the context of user queries. Recent developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI), Natural Language Processing (NLP), and Information Retrieval (IR) have introduced more advanced approaches to document search and question answering. Large Language Models (LLMs), in particular, have demonstrated the ability to understand natural language, interpret contextual information, and generate human-readable responses. Despite these capabilities, standalone language models may produce inaccurate, outdated, or unsupported information, commonly referred [PAGE 10] 2

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides an approach to addressing this limitation by combining information retrieval with the response-generation capabilities of language models. Rather than relying entirely on information learned during training, a RAG-based system first retrieves relevant information from an external document collection and then uses that information as context for generating a response. This approach allows answers to be connected to the available source material and makes the knowledge base easier to update without retraining the language model. Techniques such as Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) can combine the rankings generated by different retrieval methods, while Cross- Encoder reranking can further refine the order of retrieved passages based on their relevance to the user's question. Another important aspect of legal information retrieval is understanding the intent behind a query. Users may ask for definitions, legal rights, obligations, procedures, exceptions, comparisons, or specific facts contained in a document. In view of these requirements, this project, titled “Legal RAG: A Context-Aware Retrieval System for Document Query Answering,” focuses on developing an intelligent framework for retrieving relevant information from legal documents and generating context-aware responses. The proposed system integrates document processing, query understanding, hybrid retrieval, result fusion, Cross-Encoder reranking, language generation, and citation verification into a unified workflow.

Its purpose is to make legal information retrieval more accessible, efficient, and transparent while maintaining a connection between generated responses and the available source documents. 1.2 Problem Statement The increasing availability of digital legal information has created a need for efficient [PAGE 11] 3

CHAPTER 2 LITERATURE REVIEW

2.1 INTRODUCTION The development of intelligent document retrieval and question-answering systems has been significantly influenced by advancements in Information Retrieval (IR), Natural Language Processing (NLP), and Artificial Intelligence. These technologies enable computer systems to process large volumes of textual information, understand natural language queries, and retrieve relevant content from digital document collections. In the legal domain, efficient information retrieval is particularly important because legal information is distributed across extensive judgments, statutes, regulations, and other formal documents. Locating relevant information from these sources can be challenging due to complex terminology, lengthy documents, and the contextual nature of legal questions. Several approaches have been developed to improve document retrieval and automated question answering.

Several approaches have been developed to improve document retrieval and automated question answering. These include traditional keyword-based search, semantic retrieval, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, hybrid search, and neural reranking techniques. This chapter reviews the major concepts and research contributions relevant to the proposed Legal RAG system, examines the limitations of existing approaches, and identifies the research gap addressed by the project.

2.2 Existing Systems and Related Technologies A. Traditional Information Retrieval Traditional Information Retrieval systems identify relevant documents by matching query terms with the words present in a document collection. Two commonly used techniques are Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) and BM25. TF-IDF estimates the importance of a term by considering its frequency within a document and its distribution across the document collection. BM25, on the other hand, is a probabilistic ranking function that considers term frequency, inverse document frequency, and document length to estimate document relevance. These techniques are effective for retrieving documents containing specific keywords, legal terms, section numbers, and case references. However, they have limited ability to understand the semantic meaning of a query.

Semantic Search and Dense Retrieval Semantic search was introduced to overcome some of the limitations of conventional keyword-based retrieval. It uses embedding models to convert queries and documents into numerical vector representations that capture their semantic meaning. Dense retrieval compares the vector representations of a query and document passages using similarity measures such as cosine similarity. This allows the system to identify conceptually related information even when the exact words used in the query are not present in the document. Although semantic retrieval improves contextual matching, it may not always identify exact legal terminology, statutory references, section numbers, or case identifiers effectively.

Therefore, combining semantic retrieval with keyword-based techniques can provide a more balanced retrieval approach for legal applications. C. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines information retrieval with the natural language generation capabilities of Large Language Models. The approach was introduced in the research work Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks by Lewis et al. (2020). In a conventional language model, responses are generated primarily using knowledge acquired during training. A RAG-based system supplements this process by retrieving relevant information from an external knowledge source and providing it as context to the language model before response generation.

A RAG-based system supplements this process by retrieving relevant information from an external knowledge source and providing it as context to the language model before response generation. A typical RAG framework involves document processing, text chunking, embedding generation, document indexing, query processing, information retrieval, and context-based response generation. This approach allows the system to use domain-specific documents during answer generation and makes it possible to update the external knowledge base without retraining the entire language model. However, the effectiveness of RAG depends heavily on the quality of retrieved information. If the retrieval component selects incomplete or irrelevant passages, the generated response may also be inaccurate or insufficiently supported. D. E. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) is a ranking aggregation technique used to combine the results obtained from multiple retrieval systems. It was introduced by Cormack, Clarke, and Büttcher (2009) in their research paper Reciprocal Rank Fusion Outperforms Condorcet and Individual Rank Learning Methods. RRF combines ranked result lists by assigning scores according to the positions of documents in the individual rankings. It does not require the original relevance scores of different retrieval methods to be directly comparable. However, the retrieved passages may not always appear in the most useful order. Reranking techniques address this issue by evaluating the relevance of the retrieved passages more carefully. A generated answer may appear convincing but still contain statements that are not supported by the retrieved documents. Generated responses were validated across three checks: reference validity (matching cited IDs to retrieved chunks after case and leading-zero normalization, while accepting shortened IDs like chunk_1 only when unique across documents), claim coverage (ensuring every claim line, including wrapped bullets, carries at least one citation), and final validity (marking an answer valid only with at least one verified citation and zero unknown or uncited lines). CHAPTER 6 CONCLUSION AND FUTURE SCOPE

6.1 Conclusion This project presented the design and implementation of Legal RAG, a retrieval-augmented question-answering system for legal documents. The system extracts text from uploaded PDF documents and uses OCR when scanned pages contain insufficient extractable text. The extracted content is cleaned and divided into hierarchy-aware chunks while preserving document sections, subsection information, and relevant legal metadata. The chunks are embedded using nomic-embed-text and stored in a persistent ChromaDB collection. Legal queries are processed using dense semantic retrieval and BM25 lexical retrieval. The retrieval results are combined using Reciprocal Rank Fusion and refined using the ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 Cross-Encoder reranker. The system also classifies query intent and difficulty and adapts the retrieval effort according to question complexity. The openai/gpt-oss-20b (Groq) language model generates answers using only the retrieved context.

The openai/gpt-oss-20b (Groq) language model generates answers using only the retrieved context. The citation-verification module checks whether generated claims contain valid references to the retrieved chunks and reports missing, unknown, or partial citations. The Streamlit interface presents the answer, source passages, retrieval scores, citation status, and claim-level explainability to the user. The retrieval quality improves when semantic and lexical techniques are combined to address different types of legal queries. Answers become more transparent when the generated claims are connected to identifiable document chunks that users can inspect directly. The system should be used as an assistive legal-document search and question- answering tool. It does not replace professional legal judgment or verification against the original document and applicable law.
